analysis.one_liner: Requires water utilities to find and fully replace lead drinking-water pipes, paying the full cost themselves.
analysis.headline: Backed by a Republican sponsor and four Democrats, the bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from May 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every community water system to inventory its lead service lines — the lead pipes connecting water mains to homes — and fully replace them within ten years of an approved plan, with certified lead-removing filters on affected taps in the meantime. Water systems, not homeowners, would pay the full cost, helped by new federal money: the bill authorizes $6.6 billion a year for ten years to the drinking water state revolving fund, with $4.65 billion a year of it reserved for lead pipe replacement and priority for disadvantaged communities. Any costs not covered by that assistance could be folded into customer water rates. Lead is a neurotoxin with no known safe level, and children are the most vulnerable, which is why full pipe replacement is treated as a major public health measure.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water delivered through lead pipes — most often in older cities and neighborhoods — would get their lines fully replaced at the utility's expense, with certified lead-removing filters and cartridges on their taps until then. Children, who are most harmed by lead exposure, would benefit the most. Disadvantaged communities would get priority for the federal loan and grant assistance, and pipe-replacement contractors and filter manufacturers would gain a decade of mandated work.

how_it_helps.text: Every community water system must fully replace all of its lead service lines within 10 years of plan approval, and partial replacement is banned except in emergencies, which must be followed by full replacement within 90 days.
Systems serving 3,300 or more people must submit an inventory-and-replacement plan to the EPA within 1 year and complete their inventories within 3 years; small systems get 5 years for both.

Until replacement is done, systems must install NSF-certified lead-reducing filters on every primary drinking tap served by a lead line and keep supplying replacement cartridges, at the system's expense.
Homeowners do not pay: the water system pays the full cost of every replacement and filter, and replacement can only be skipped for a line the property owner personally declines.

The bill authorizes $6.6 billion per year for fiscal 2022–2031 to the drinking water state revolving fund, with $4.65 billion per year reserved for lead service line replacement and priority given to disadvantaged communities.

The EPA can enforce the replacement requirements directly even in states that normally run their own drinking water programs, and systems can only get extra time by holding a public hearing and proving more than 100,000 lead lines make the deadline infeasible.

analysis.who_pays: Community water systems would bear the full cost of inventories, replacements, and filters. Where federal and state assistance does not cover the cost, systems may fold it into their rate base — meaning customer water bills could rise, including in the older, often lower-income communities with the most lead lines. Most of the federal help authorized here flows as loans and loan guarantees that must be repaid, and federal taxpayers would fund the appropriations: $10 million a year for EPA administration and $6.6 billion a year for ten years for the revolving fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Water utilities, their customers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Systems may incorporate replacement and filter costs not covered by grants into their rates, so water bills could rise — and the communities with the most lead lines are often the ones least able to absorb higher bills.
Most of the dedicated federal assistance is revolving-fund loans and loan guarantees, not grants, so utilities would be taking on debt that ultimately gets repaid through rates.
Only $10 million a year is authorized for EPA administration and oversight, thin funding for policing compliance with a nationwide replacement mandate.

The 10-year deadline is firm: only systems with more than 100,000 known or suspected lead lines can even apply for an extension, and only for the minimum time necessary — a hard pace for some large older systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: lead in drinking water has no known safe level and harms children's development, and the bill's design is fair — it puts costs on water systems and federal funds rather than individual homeowners, bans partial replacement, requires interim filters, and prioritizes disadvantaged communities. The honest costs are that uncovered costs and loan repayments can still land on water bills, and oversight funding is modest. On balance the trade favors the public; the weakest part of the design is relying on repayable loans for a task this large.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it down to its environment subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Smith (R-NJ) introduced the bill on May 18, 2021 for himself and Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX).
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day.
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no one opposed it on the record at any point.
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded — the last action of record is the May 19, 2021 subcommittee referral — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water utilities avoided a federal deadline to replace their lead lines at their own expense, and their ratepayers avoided the rate increases the mandate could have brought. People still drinking water through lead lines got no new replacement deadline from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Get the Lead Out Act on May 18, 2021.

for.name: Rep. Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Joined Smith as the bill's co-introducer when it was filed.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took up the bill only to refer it to the Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, which never held a hearing or markup; no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and a Democrat co-introduced it, with three more Democratic cosponsors — five supporters in a 435-member House — and no recorded opposition, because the bill never got far enough for a vote.

industries.note: The bill orders every community water system to find and fully replace its lead service lines and pay the full cost, including filters — but it also sends them billions a year in dedicated federal revolving-fund money with priority for disadvantaged communities, and lets systems fold uncovered costs into customer rates. The industry's cost-avoidance interest runs against the public's interest in lead-free water, though the federal funding softens the burden.
A mandated full replacement of every lead service line within about a decade of plan approval, backed by federal loan money, means a sustained decade of digging and replacement work.
Certified lead-reducing filters and ongoing replacement cartridges would be mandatory on every tap served by a lead line until replacement is complete — a large guaranteed market.
